senses: The mind; that which distinguishes man from the animals.
ety: From Sanskrit मनस् (manas, “mind”). Doublet of mind.

senses: One who makes keys.
ety: From Middle English kay maker, equivalent to key + maker.

senses: A piece of jewelry/jewellery, resembling a bracelet but worn around the ankle.
An ankle sock.
A type of mulled wine from German-speaking countries made from red wine with cinnamon and other herbs and spices.
bureau de change; currency exchange
ety: Borrowed from Spanish or Portuguese cambio.

senses: a denomination, sect, church, or other group which professes to be Christian but uses water to administer the Eucharist instead of wine.
The concept that everything is organic, or forms part of an organic whole.
The treatment of society or the universe as if it were an organism.
The mereological idea that living things are the only composite objects.
The theory that the total organization of an organism is more important than the functioning of its individual organs.
examples: Its asymmetrical design, half curved, half rectangular, reflects the marquise's divided nature: female organicism joined to male geometry, a psychic hermaphroditism.

senses: Being or relating to a donation.
ety: From Latin dōnātīvum (“a gratuity”), from dōnō (“to give [a present]”), from dōnum (“gift”).

senses: A flexible branch or twig of a plant such as willow, used in weaving baskets and furniture.
ety: From Middle English wiker, cognate with Old Swedish vikker (“willow”), Old Norse veikr (“weak”), English weak.

senses: a person who makes models, especially from a plastic medium such as clay
a person who models the behaviour of a physical system, especially by using a computer model
Synonym of axletree.
ety: From axle + rod, modelled after axletree, axlepin, etc.
examples: An unreasonable urge told me to get away from the noise—to get away from the thousand little talks of wives and kids, policemen and weigh stations, axlerods and tires.

senses: Producing obstruction due to inflammation and fibrosis.
ety: From Latin oblitterare (“to hide writing”), from ob (“out”) + littera (“letter”).
examples: Dr Adam explained that the phimosis was caused by balanitis xerotica obliterans

senses: Abounding in cliffs.
Characteristic of a cliff.
An oriental plane tree (Platanus orientalis).
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi चिनार (cinār) / Urdu چِنَار (cinār), in turn derived from Classical Persian چِنَار (činār, “Platanus”), ultimately derived from Middle Persian cynʾl (/⁠činār⁠/).
examples: The lakes, the gardens, the chinars golden in autumn, the Himalayas all around.
I too felt that the government has not made judicious use of its powers to curb the felling of chinars.

senses: The quality of being irreversible; the lack of an ability to be reversed.
A thin mortar used to fill the gaps between tiles and cavities in masonry.
ety: From Middle English growte, grut, from Old English grūt (“dregs; coarse meal”), from Proto-West Germanic *grūt, from Proto-Germanic *grūtą (compare Dutch gruit (“dregs”), German Grauß, Norwegian grut (“ground”)), lengthening of Proto-Germanic *grutą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to grind, rub”). Related to grit.

senses: Someone who studies at a seminary.
One who follows a philosophical belief in a naked, natural life and prefers to live without clothes, often for reasons of ecology, health, religious belief, and/or ethical concerns.
One who believes in the doctrine of naturism, which attributes everything to nature.
To conceptualize afresh; to develop a replacement concept of.
To be played rather fast and lively.
ety: Borrowed from Italian allegretto, diminutive form of allegro.

senses: A round of a ladder.
A stave in the side of a wagon.
A large pole by which barges are propelled against the stream; a poy.
ety: From Middle English stoure, stourre, from Old Norse staurr (“a stake, pale”), from Proto-Germanic *stauraz (“pole, support”), from Proto-Indo-European *stā- (“to stand, place”). Cognate with Icelandic staur (“a stake, pole”), Ancient Greek σταυρός (staurós, “a stake, cross”).

senses: A fire whirl (a whirling column of fire found in large fiery areas such as wildfires, similar in appearance to a tornado made out of fire).
A true tornado generated by a firestorm.
ety: Blend of fire + tornado. By surface analysis, fire + -nado.

senses: A rarely used typographical symbol of three asterisks arranged in a triangle, ⁂, used to call attention to a passage or to separate subchapters in a book. Distinct from a dinkus which also uses asterisks to separate.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἀστερισμός (asterismós, “a group of stars”), from ἀστήρ (astḗr, “star”). Analyzable as aster- + -ism.

senses: The act of rendering someone or something masculine.
examples: A pseudohermaphroditic infant female rhesus monkey (Macaca mulatta) showing masculinization of the external genitalia as a result of exposure to testosterone propionate during foetal development.

senses: Capable of being skipped.
Not worth watching or doing; missable.
A mixed woodland-grassland biome and ecosystem characterised by the trees being sufficiently widely spaced so that the canopy does not close.
A Japanese wooden doll with a spherical head having simple painted-on features, and a limbless, cylindrical body, typically featuring a painted-on floral design.
examples: The popularity of kokeshi among Japanese tourists today is thus an eloquent testimony to the survival of a folk tradition as well as to the modern generation's ignorance of its implications.

The addition of decorative clothing a la simple rings of color and the expressive, even suggestive, faces that so many kokeshi wear, turned them from simple children's toys into works of collectible folk art.

senses: A medieval manuscript register containing full or excerpted transcriptions of important documents, especially of originally loose, single-sheet charters.
A collection of original documents bound in one volume.
An officer who had charge of records or other public papers.
ety: From Middle English cartulari, borrowed from Medieval Latin chartulārium. Doublet of khaltura.

senses: A plastic shell that lines the bed of a vehicle.
examples: Pickup truck bedliners are durable high-density molded polyethylene inserts that slip over the exposed cargo bed.

Even when you order your late - model pickup with a drop-in plastic bedliner from the factory, you might experience rust buildup between the plastic bedliner and the sheet metal of the truck bed after a few years.

senses: Somewhat dun, dusky brownish.
ety: From dun (“dusky brown”) + -y (“forming adjectives of lesser degree”).

senses: A soldier, in Spanish-speaking contexts.
The tendency of a person to commit suicide.
A fatality that is an instance of suicide.
The principal part of a duet.
ety: Borrowed from Italian primo (“first”). Doublet of prime and primus.

senses: That causes photosensitization
A man who carries a flag, especially one used for signalling.
A man who raises a flag.
examples: At the approach to Southampton Terminus, double track branches off to the left, runs alongside the platforms and then cuts across Canute Road on an open crossing under the protection of a flagman.

senses: A unit of measurement used in particular for smoke detectors which respond to absorption of light by smoke, in percent absorption per unit length, e.g. % obs/ft, % obs/m.
ety: From Latin obscūrātiō. By surface analysis, obscure + -ation.

senses: Synonym of cisgender.
A machine that forms material into granules.
Something that descrambles; a device for decoding a scrambled signal.
A redfin shiner (Lythrurus umbratilis), of the central US.
ety: From red + fin, having a red dorsal fin, especially males in the breeding season.
